title: Ginger
subtitle: The kitchen rhizome for nausea, cold days, and a sluggish digestion
excerpt: Ginger is the dried or fresh rhizome kept in almost every kitchen. Traditionally taken for nausea, poor circulation, and cramping digestion, it crosses western herbal, Chinese, and Ayurvedic traditions. A jar of dried ginger keeps two years in a cupboard.

glossaryTerms.definition: A medicine that slows blood clotting. Examples include warfarin and aspirin. Herbs with antiplatelet activity can add to the effect.
A horizontal underground stem that sends out roots and shoots. Ginger, turmeric, and galangal are all rhizomes, not true roots.
An action that reduces nausea and the urge to vomit. Ginger is the most widely studied plant with this traditional reputation.

content.text: Ginger in the home kitchen: the dried powder in biscuits, the fresh
rhizome

grated into a cup of hot water, the slice steeped in a teapot for nausea. Three traditions and several thousand years of kitchen medicine rely on the same part: the thick, knobbly underground stem. Western herbal, Chinese, and Ayurvedic practices all reach for it, each with its own emphasis, but the ground shared between them is wide. A jar of dried ginger powder or sliced dried root keeps two years in a cool cupboard.
Precautions
Not medical advice. Consult a qualified herbalist or doctor for ongoing or serious symptoms.
Drug interactions: ginger has mild
anticoagulant

activity. Readers on warfarin, aspirin, clopidogrel, or any other blood-thinning medicine should keep ginger to culinary levels and consult their prescriber before using therapeutic doses. The antiplatelet effect of ginger is mild at kitchen quantities but becomes relevant at concentrated alcohol extract or high-dose supplement levels.

Pregnancy: culinary use and small medicinal teas using up to 1 g of dried ginger per cup are widely documented for morning sickness and are generally regarded as reasonable at that dose. Doses above 2 g per day sit in the cautious column in pregnancy. Consult a herbalist or your midwife before regular therapeutic use in pregnancy.
Botanical

Zingiber officinale, family Zingiberaceae. The part used is the rhizome: the fleshy underground stem harvested after the aerial shoots die back, typically in autumn. Fresh rhizomes are the familiar rough-skinned, pale-yellow lumps sold in every supermarket. Dried rhizomes are either whole, sliced, or ground. Ground ginger and sliced dried ginger have different flavour and constituent profiles: drying converts some of the gingerols to shogaols, which are sharper and more warming in character. The plant is tropical in origin and grown commercially across South Asia, West Africa, and the Caribbean. It does not naturalise in the UK climate but is easy to grow in a pot given warmth and moisture.
active compounds and actions

The primary active compounds of fresh ginger are gingerols, pungent compounds that give fresh ginger its bite. Drying converts them partly to shogaols, which are stronger in warmth and pungency. Zingiberene carries most of the aromatic quality. These compounds are linked to the wind-easing action, the circulatory warming effect, and the best-studied action: easing nausea. Limited trial evidence supports the use for morning sickness and post-operative nausea. The calms swelling action comes from gingerol effects on prostaglandin pathways, but the effect at kitchen doses is modest.
Traditional uses

Western herbal practice has used ginger for digestive complaints since at least the medieval period. The primary applications are nausea (morning sickness, travel sickness, post-operative nausea). Sluggish digestion and trapped wind, and as a warming herb in cold or damp conditions, especially respiratory complaints where warming the circulation is part of the approach. Ginger tea was the household remedy for a cramping gut and for anyone feeling cold to the bone.

Chinese herbal medicine distinguishes between fresh ginger (sheng jiang) and dried ginger (gan jiang). The terms come from Chinese medicine names. Fresh ginger is used to warm the stomach, stop vomiting, and promote gentle sweating in the first stages of a cold. Dried ginger is considered more intensely warming and is used to warm the interior, especially the stomach and lungs in cold-deficiency patterns. The distinction between fresh and dried forms as therapeutically different preparations is a specific feature of the Chinese tradition not always carried into western herbal use.

Ayurvedic medicine knows ginger as sunthi (dried) and adrak (fresh), both key spices in Ayurvedic cooking. The tradition uses ginger to help digestion, ease nausea, reduce mucus accumulation in the respiratory tract. And as a general circulatory warming herb. Ginger forms the base of the classical Ayurvedic formula trikatu alongside long pepper and black pepper. Used for sluggish digestion and cold presentations.
Preparations

The simplest preparation is a hot infusion: one to two teaspoons of dried sliced ginger or a two-centimetre piece of fresh ginger grated into a cup, covered with just-off-boil water, and steeped covered for ten minutes. The cover matters: the volatile aromatic fraction is the part that escapes into steam and is lost from an uncovered cup. Strain before drinking.

For a stronger preparation from the dried root or where the fresh root is unavailable, a simmered preparation is more effective: simmer sliced dried ginger gently in water for fifteen minutes, covered, then strain. This draws more from the woody cell walls of dried root than a simple steep does.

Ginger alcohol extract in 40% spirit is made by macerating 1 part dried ginger to 5 parts spirit by weight for four to six weeks. It is a concentrated preparation used in small doses (1 to 2 ml) rather than by the cup. Dried ginger powder stirred into warm water or honey is a traditional home remedy across several cultures and is the fastest kitchen preparation when dried powder is all that is to hand.
Cautions and cautions

Anticoagulant medicines: ginger has mild antiplatelet activity. At cooking amounts this is rarely a concern. At concentrated extract or supplement doses, anyone on warfarin, aspirin, or blood-thinning medicines should speak to their prescriber. The risk is additive, not dramatic.

Pregnancy at high doses: small medicinal teas using up to 1 g dried ginger per cup have been used for morning sickness in the first trimester and are widely regarded in the herbal literature as reasonable at that dose. Doses above 2 g per day are in the cautious column. Consult a herbalist or your midwife before regular therapeutic doses in pregnancy.

Gastric sensitivity: in a small number of readers ginger at strong doses causes heartburn or gastric irritation. This is most common on an empty stomach. Start with a weak tea and see how it sits before increasing the dose.
